background.title: Looking at your own work honestly
background.html:
It is hard to see mistakes in your own writing: you read what you meant, not what you wrote. Two tricks help.

  • Read your paragraph one sentence at a time and ask of each: what does this sentence do? Describe, name, explain, judge?
  • Compare with a model sentence by sentence, not as a whole.

A habit is a mistake that comes back every time. Once you can name it, you can catch it.

background.title: What an infographic is
background.html:
An infographic (information + graphic) shows facts as a picture: big numbers, small icons, colours and arrows, with very few words. You see posters like this in schools, hospitals and on social media.

It looks neutral, like a list of facts, but someone chose every number, colour and arrow. In Paper 1 you analyse those choices exactly as you did for cartoons.

background.title: Numbers in plain words
background.html:
"6 out of 10" means 60%: of every 10 people, 6. A proportion is this kind of part of a whole.

"An estimated 1 million" means experts calculated it carefully from data; it is not an exact count of every person.

You do not need to check or argue with the numbers in Paper 1. You analyse how they are shown: how big, what colour, next to what.

background.title: Who made it: the WHO
background.html:
The World Health Organization (WHO) is the United Nations agency for health: countries work together through it on things like vaccines, diseases and healthy living. It has regional offices; today's infographic comes from its office for Europe.

Who made a text matters: a health agency's logo makes readers trust the message more than an unknown website's would.

terms.def: Writing down everything you remember about a topic on a blank page, fast and without notes, before checking.
The tab in your study sheet where you write every lost mark, its type and the rule that fixes it.
The standards your answer is marked against. Paper 1 has four, A to D, each worth 5 marks per text.
Not seen before. In Paper 1 the texts are new to you, so you prepare a method, not answers.
Not a novel, poem or play. Everyday texts such as adverts, speeches, blogs, photographs, infographics and cartoons.
Belonging to literature: novels, poems, plays, short stories and, for the IB, graphic novels.
The kind of text, such as an advert, a speech, an infographic or a cartoon. Each type has its own usual features.
The question printed with each Paper 1 text. It points you to one aspect of how the text works; keep coming back to it.
Your class method for each point: spot a choice, explain it (name the technique), say its effect on the reader, link it to the purpose.
Your class annotation tool: five groups of questions (Audience, Meaning, Feeling, Craft, Shape) to ask about any text.
The 20 out of 20 model answer in your class files, on a 2020 cartoon by David Horsey. Studied on 13 November.
A mistake you make again and again in the same way, such as stopping after naming a technique.
What a text suggests without saying it directly. You work it out from clues.
The plain surface meaning: what is actually shown or said, before any reading between the lines.
Your reasoned idea of what a text means beyond the obvious, supported by details from it.
Judging how well something works, with reasons: is this choice effective, and why?
Clear and logical: each sentence follows from the one before, so the whole makes sense as one argument.
Small, less obvious details or meanings that a careful reader notices.
Only saying what is there, without explaining how it creates meaning. The IB marks this low in criterion B.
How formal the language is, and whose kind of voice it sounds like. Exam answers need a formal register.
Your main point, stated in one sentence that answers the guiding question. Every other sentence then supports it.
In satire, the person, group or idea being criticised.
Verbs that say what a choice does: exposes, ridicules, undermines, invites, positions, implicates, provokes, disarms, reinforces, challenges.
Placing two contrasting things side by side so the reader compares them.
A drawing of a real person with some features stretched or shrunk to make a point.
Words that mean, or hide, the opposite of what they say: "lovely weather" in a storm.
A joke using a word or phrase with two meanings at once.
In comics, the reader's mind joining separate panels into one story and filling in what is not drawn.
The empty strip between two comic panels, where time passes.
A text that shows information as a picture: big numbers, icons, colours and arrows, with few words.
A fact given as a number, such as "6 out of 10" or "1 million".
A row of small icons standing for a number: 10 little people with 3 coloured in shows 3 out of 10.
A simple picture of the thing itself, such as a bus for transport.
A thing that stands for an idea, such as a heart for love or a dove for peace.
Giving each section or idea its own colour, so the reader groups and follows information easily.
Lines, arrows or numbers that lead the eye through a text in the order the creator wants.
A verb form that gives an order or instruction: "Use the stairs", "Drink more water".
The small design that stands for an organisation, like a badge. It tells you who made the text.
A group of three words, phrases or short sentences in a row, which sounds complete and is easy to remember.
The part of a persuasive text that tells the audience exactly what to do now.
A part of a whole, such as 3 out of 4.
A word or phrase that links ideas, such as parce que (because) or grâce à (thanks to).
Your own collection of notes, analyses and reflections from the course. It is not graded, but you use it to prepare for assessments.
An essay that compares two texts: how they are alike and different, and why. In Paper 2, two literary works you studied.
A 15-minute spoken assessment with your teacher: 10 minutes on how a global issue is shown in two texts you studied, then 5 minutes of questions.
A 1,200 to 1,500 word essay you write during the course, only at Higher Level, on one text or body of work you studied.
